questions.title: What does 'sufficiency of an indictment' mean during a de novo review?
questions.question_body: I'm confused about the procedural standard here. The court says it reviews the sufficiency of the indictment 'de novo' and is required to 'take the allegations of the indictment as true.' Does this mean the court is not allowed to question whether the defendants actually did anything wrong, but only whether the written charges are worded specifically enough to meet the legal elements of the crime?

questions.title: What is the legal distinction between the 'right-to-control' theory and the 'fraudulent-inducement' theory?
questions.question_body: The court spends a lot of time distinguishing this case from Ciminelli. In Ciminelli, the government lost because they tried to prove fraud based on the 'right-to-control' theory (depriving someone of info). In this case, the court says the government is using 'fraudulent-inducement.' Can someone explain the practical difference? If a defendant lies to an investor about a stock price, isn't that depriving them of information? Why does the theory they use to describe the lie change whether the charge is valid?

questions.title: How can there be a fraud conviction if the victim didn't suffer a 'net pecuniary loss'?
questions.question_body: I'm struggling with the court's application of Kousisis. The opinion says that a defendant can be convicted even if they don't leave the victim economically worse off, as long as they 'obtain' the victim's money or property. In this 'pump and dump' scheme, the followers are buying securities. If the securities are of 'market value,' and the followers still own those securities, how did the defendants 'obtain' anything from the followers? It feels like the followers just traded cash for a stock, but it doesn't seem like the followers were actually 'deprived' of their property.

questions.title: Why is the court 'borrowing' concepts from mail and wire fraud for a securities fraud statute?
questions.question_body: The opinion notes there is 'scant caselaw' for 18 U.S.C. § 1348 (securities fraud) and explains that the court is relying on mail and wire fraud precedents instead. Does this mean that the definition of 'securities fraud' is essentially just 'mail/wire fraud' with a different victim? Are there any specific elements of securities fraud that are being ignored or simplified by using these other statutes as a proxy?

questions.title: At what point in a 'pump and dump' scheme is the 'object' of the fraud actually obtained?
questions.question_body: The court says a fraud is complete when the defendant 'induced the deprivation of money or property.' In a pump and dump, the defendants lie to 'pump' the price (inducing followers to buy) and then they 'dump' (sell) their own shares. Does the 'object' of the fraud (the money/property) count as being 'obtained' at the moment the followers buy the stock, or is the 'object' the profit the defendants make when they sell their shares? I'm trying to understand which specific act in the timeline the court is identifying as the 'fraudulent-inducement.'
